articles.title: Sign Off the Promises, Not the Paragraphs: A Claim-Strength Linter for Model-Drafted Docs
articles.excerpt: A model can draft your walkthrough, your config table, and most of your troubleshooting prose, but it must never be the last author of a sentence that promises behavior. That single rule is the whole…
articles.body: A model can draft your walkthrough, your config table, and most of your troubleshooting prose, but it must never be the last author of a sentence that promises behavior. That single rule is the whole workflow below: the model owns procedure, a human owns promises, and a small linter decides which sentences count as promises. Everything else here is machinery for enforcing that split on every pull request. The artifact is two files and about eighty lines of Python. One file inventories promise-bearing sentences and scores their strength; the other records a human sign-off with a live evidence pointer for each one. Existing doc tooling usually validates links, spelling, or style, so it happily ships a sentence that claims an operation is atomic when nothing tests atomicity. 1.

articles.title: Skip Is Not a Freeze: Revocable Seeded Freezes for Agent Patches
articles.excerpt: A skipped test is not a frozen test. It is a deleted test that still compiles. The difference matters the moment an agent starts shipping patches into the same suite, because a skip has no expiry, no…
articles.body: A skipped test is not a frozen test. It is a deleted test that still compiles. The difference matters the moment an agent starts shipping patches into the same suite, because a skip has no expiry, no signature, and no obligation to ever come back. This post describes a freeze that revokes itself: every frozen test carries the seed that reproduces its failure, and every agent patch must re-run that seed and classify the result. If the seeded run now fails deterministically, the freeze is void — that is a regression, not flake. All code below is a reference implementation. I have not run it against a production repository, so treat the thresholds and the signature function as starting points you calibrate on your own suite.

articles.title: MCP tool authorization: a gateway deny counts only when the server shows no side effect
articles.excerpt: Putting a gateway in front of an MCP server gives you a policy enforcement point on one network path. It does not prove the upstream server cannot be reached another way. A test that stops at the gate…
articles.body: Putting a gateway in front of an MCP server gives you a policy enforcement point on one network path. It does not prove the upstream server cannot be reached another way. A test that stops at the gateway's decision log checks the gateway's claim against the gateway's own records: the request was denied, the log says so, test passed. The question that matters is different: can a call the policy denies still cause a side effect on the upstream server? You answer that at the server and in the state it changes. This article proposes a test matrix built around that one assertion, with a harmless fixture server that keeps two records: one of every call its handlers receive, and one of the state it actually changed.

articles.body: A refactor is only as safe as its smallest revertible step. If nobody can undo your change with one command, the characterization suite is decoration. This post starts after the tests are green. It covers cutting the change, ordering the cuts, and proving each commit stands alone. The contract: green and revertible at every commit Two properties per commit. The suite is green. git revert <sha> restores green with no hand edits. Most teams check the first property only at the branch tip. That is not enough. A broken middle commit blocks git bisect and forces a full rollback later. Step 1 — Print a per-commit ledger Run this before you ask for review.

articles.title: An AI poller cost us almost 27 USD in one day: the 40-line spend guard we added
articles.excerpt: One day in July our AI bill reached almost 27 USD in a single day. Nobody had asked for it. This post is the short version of what went wrong and the small guard we run so it does not happen silently…
articles.body: One day in July our AI bill reached almost 27 USD in a single day. Nobody had asked for it. This post is the short version of what went wrong and the small guard we run so it does not happen silently again. The code is about 40 lines of Python with no extra packages. What happened We had an agent task that woke up every 3 minutes to check an inbox. Each wake-up was a full model call. The scheduler had registered that task 4 times, so it really ran about 80 times an hour. That alone would have been cheap, because the task used a free model. Then the free model started answering with rate limit errors (HTTP 429). Our model router had a fallback list, and the next entry was a paid model. Every 429 quietly became a paid call. Nothing watched the spend, so we only saw it hours later.

articles.body: From 1980 until 1995, cartoonist Gary Larson wrote and drew The Far Side . It was a single panel comic strip filled with non-sequitur, surreal jokes mostly aimed at adults instead of children, which was unusual for newspaper comics at the time. Also unusual was the fact that, unlike most daily comic strips, The Far Side had no recurring characters. Peanuts has its gang of kids and Garfield has its cast of humans and animals, but every panel of The Far Side introduces new characters and scenarios all aimed at delivering one single joke.

articles.excerpt: Lots of Redshirts are going to die
articles.body: Generating creature tokens is a common way to make the most out of your resources in a game of Magic: The Gathering . They can be sacrificed for powerful effects, used to chump block , or amassed to overwhelm your opponent. Cards typically generate tokens of the same color, like white Warriors for Secure the Wastes , green Squirrels for Deranged Hermit , and black Zombies for Ghoulish Procession . Yet numerous cards in Magic: The Gathering Star Trek generate 1/1 red Officer tokens regardless of the base color, from the white Captain Benjamin Sisko to the green MACO Strike Team . The discrepancy is a nod to the sci-fi franchise’s darkest running joke.

articles.body: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman is serious about launching "big rockets" to the moon every single year for the agency's Artemis program. And the new space race with China is fueling that ambition. "I feel good. I feel like we are certainly on a more achievable path to the lunar surface today than where we were before," Isaacman told Space.com. We recently sat down with the NASA chief to discuss the state of the Artemis program , and, off the bat, he made it clear that he's confident in the U.S. space program following the success of April's Artemis II mission around the moon. articles.title: Starlink Mobile: All the news on SpaceX’s major mobile carrier ambitions
articles.excerpt: SpaceX has declared that it’s going to make Starlink Mobile a “major” mobile carrier. The Elon Musk-owned company has already deployed thousands of direct-to-cell satellites, but its next big challeng…
articles.body: SpaceX has declared that it’s going to make Starlink Mobile a “major” mobile carrier. The Elon Musk-owned company has already deployed thousands of direct-to-cell satellites, but its next big challenge is building out its 5G network here on Earth. As part of its plans to rival AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile, SpaceX has inked a deal with Qualcomm , which will deploy its cellular technology across tens of thousands of 5G cell sites starting in 2027. SpaceX is also reportedly in talks to buy Boost Mobile , potentially allowing it to launch Starlink Mobile through the service. Another report suggests SpaceX may tap into 80,000 cell sites across the US to build out its network. SpaceX’s big plans have garnered some reactions in the telecom industry.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 6, 1572: A German astronomer discovers the Tycho supernova with the naked eye, but everyone thought the cosmic explosion was a 'new star'
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova later caleld the Tycho supernova with his bare eyes. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova with his bare eyes. He spotted the exploding star in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was as bright as Venus and could even be seen during the day. Astronomers were really confused, because it looked like a star just appeared out of nowhere. Schulër may have been the first to see it, but the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe is widely credited for the discovery. Brahe studied it in detail and wrote a whole book about this so-called "new star." It then became known as "Tycho's Star." At the time, supernovas had not yet been discovered. Tycho's Star was finally classified as a supernova in the 1940s. Scientists now think it was a small star called a white dwarf that exploded thousands of years ago.

articles.title: AST SpaceMobile announces new 'Blacklift' rocket, targets 2028 launch debut
articles.excerpt: AST SpaceMobile plans to launch its broadband satellites on a new rocket called Blacklift, which it will build in house and plans to start flying in 2028.
articles.body: Another new private rocket is in the works. AST SpaceMobile announced today (Nov. 6) that it's building a reusable rocket called Blacklift to launch its broadband satellites to low Earth orbit (LEO), with first flight targeted in 2028. The news comes just 10 days after Cowboy Space unveiled Big Iron , a rocket designed to launch its constellation of 20,000 AI data centers . Cowboy Space is also targeting 2028 for its first liftoff. "The Blacklift rocket is the springboard to significantly expand our total addressable market, providing AST SpaceMobile with regular unconstrained access to orbit and providing for most favorable owners’ economics in the industry," Abel Avellan, the company's founder, chairman and CEO, said in a statement today .

articles.title: Chainalysis says hackers stole credentials and tokens for all of its customers
articles.excerpt: Company said a "multifront cyberattack" included AI agents and an on-path data snatch.
articles.body: Blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis said that hackers have obtained sensitive personal information—including names, usernames, password hashes, and live tokens—for all of its users following a breach of its network security. The accomplishment could be a major coup for the attackers. Both Chainalysis and public sources have revealed a long list of high-profile customers, including government agencies such as the FBI, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, and the US Air Force, as well as private companies such as Microsoft, Coinbase, and Barclays. It's unclear if the data theft exposed customers to additional threats. We regret to inform you...
